title: Peoria
name: Peoria
metaTitle: 1031 Exchange Peoria AZ | 1031 Exchange of Phoenix
metaDescription: Peoria 1031 exchange coordination for P83 entertainment district, Loop 101 industrial, and Lake Pleasant corridor owners in the northwest Valley.

sections.html: Peoria has grown from a quiet bedroom community into a city with a genuine entertainment district, a real industrial base, and a recreation-driven corridor up toward Lake Pleasant, all inside the same city limits. A seller here should be specific about which of those three markets their property sits in, because pricing logic differs across all three.

sections.heading: P83 Has Become the Northwest Valley's Entertainment Anchor
sections.html:
The P83 district around 83rd Avenue, developed alongside the Peoria Sports Complex spring training facility, has pulled in restaurants, breweries, and entertainment concepts that draw from well beyond Peoria's own borders during spring training season and stay busy on weekends the rest of the year. A buyer should ask specifically how much of a tenant's revenue concentrates in the spring months, since that seasonal bump does not carry evenly across the full year.

Weeknight traffic outside of spring training deserves its own line item in any pro forma, since a district built primarily around a six-week baseball calendar needs a genuine secondary demand driver to perform well the other ten months.

sections.heading: Loop 101 Industrial Keeps Pace With Statewide Distribution Demand
sections.html:
Distribution and light industrial buildings along the Loop 101 corridor in Peoria benefit from the same statewide logistics growth reshaping Goodyear and Glendale, though land here costs less and buildings tend to be smaller. That makes Peoria industrial attractive to a buyer who wants exposure to the sector without competing directly against the large institutional players active around the Loop 303.

Smaller building size cuts both ways. It keeps entry pricing manageable for a mid-size exchange buyer, but it also means fewer national logistics tenants are candidates, so a seller should expect a more regional, owner-user-heavy tenant pool than the mega-distribution stock farther west.

sections.heading: Retail Follows a Steady, Broad-Based Rooftop Curve
sections.html: Peoria's population has grown steadily rather than in the sharp bursts seen in some of the far West Valley cities, and its retail centers reflect that, generally leasing to grocery anchors, medical tenants, and everyday service businesses rather than to a fast-changing mix of new concepts chasing new subdivisions. This makes retail income here comparatively easy to underwrite, though it also means growth in rents tends to be gradual rather than dramatic. A center leaning too heavily on grocery and everyday service tenants without any medical or specialty draw can also feel undifferentiated next to newer competition, so tenant mix diversity is worth checking alongside the occupancy number.

sections.heading: The Lake Pleasant Corridor Is a Different Kind of Investment
sections.html:
Land and small commercial buildings along the Lake Pleasant Parkway corridor north of the city serve a recreation-driven customer base tied to boating and lake traffic, and demand there can be genuinely seasonal in a way the rest of Peoria is not. A buyer used to a conventional suburban lease pattern should not assume this corridor behaves the same way.

Replacement candidates a buyer will typically encounter across the city include:

  • Restaurant and entertainment space in the P83 district near the sports complex
  • Distribution and light industrial buildings along the Loop 101 corridor
  • Grocery-anchored neighborhood retail serving established residential areas
  • Medical office tied to the city's growing hospital and clinic base
  • Recreation-oriented retail and land along the Lake Pleasant Parkway corridor

Boat storage and marine service uses along the Lake Pleasant corridor deserve a separate look as well, since they serve a narrower but fairly loyal customer base tied directly to the lake rather than to ordinary retail foot traffic.

sections.heading: Match the Identification List to the Seasonality You're Trading
sections.html: A seller exiting P83 entertainment property should build in extra identification candidates through the 200% rule, since that niche has a smaller buyer pool than ordinary retail. A seller exiting steady neighborhood retail or Loop 101 industrial usually has an easier time sticking with the three-property rule, since those categories trade in more predictable, comparable patterns across the city.

faqs.q: How much does spring training season affect P83 entertainment district income?
faqs.a: It can concentrate a meaningful share of annual revenue into the spring months, so a buyer should ask for revenue broken out by season rather than relying on a flat annualized figure that could overstate typical performance the rest of the year.

faqs.q: Is Loop 101 industrial in Peoria comparable to industrial near Goodyear?
faqs.a: It benefits from the same statewide logistics demand, but land and building prices in Peoria are generally lower, and buildings tend to be smaller. That makes it a reasonable entry point for a buyer who wants industrial exposure without competing against larger institutional deals farther southwest.

faqs.q: Why is retail income in established Peoria neighborhoods easier to underwrite?
faqs.a: Population growth here has been steady rather than sudden, and centers tend to lease to grocery, medical, and everyday service tenants rather than a fast-rotating mix chasing new subdivisions. That produces more predictable, if slower-growing, rent trends.

faqs.q: Does property near Lake Pleasant behave like the rest of Peoria's commercial market?
faqs.a: No. Demand along the Lake Pleasant Parkway corridor is tied to recreational boating and lake traffic and can be genuinely seasonal, unlike the steadier suburban lease patterns found closer to the city's core.

faqs.q: Can 1031 Exchange of Phoenix confirm my Peoria property qualifies for exchange treatment?
faqs.a: No. This service coordinates identification, scheduling, and communication among the investor's advisors. Whether a specific property and transaction qualify as like-kind is a determination made by the investor's own tax advisor and qualified intermediary.
